claim: The thymus was devoid of myeloid cells co-expressing CD11b and Gr-1 despite high systemic MDSC burdens in 4T1 tumor-bearing BALB/c female mice.
source: We found the thymus was devoid of myeloid cells co-expressing the canonical murine MDSC markers CD11b and Gr-1 despite high systemic MDSC burdens in 4T1 tumor-bearing BALB/c female mice (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data shown in Figure 1A demonstrating absence of CD11b+Gr-1+ cells in thymus of 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: L-selectin was not altered on thymic naïve CD4+CD44lo and CD8+CD44lo T cells in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice when compared to non-tumor bearing controls.
source: Moreover, L-selectin was not altered on thymic naïve CD4+CD44lo and CD8+CD44lo T cells when compared to non-tumor bearing controls (NTB).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis shown in Figure 1A comparing L-selectin expression on thymic T cells between NTB and 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: MDSC were rare in peripheral LN (pLN) of 4T1-bearing mice, including tumor-draining inguinal LN.
source: MDSC were also rare in peripheral LN (pLN) of 4T1-bearing mice, including tumor-draining inguinal LN, which correlated with the absence of L-selectin modulation on naïve T cells at these sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 1A showing low percentages of CD11b+Gr-1+ cells in pLN and inguinal LN.

claim: L-selectin modulation was absent on naïve T cells in peripheral and tumor-draining inguinal lymph nodes of 4T1-bearing mice.
source: MDSC were also rare in peripheral LN (pLN) of 4T1-bearing mice, including tumor-draining inguinal LN, which correlated with the absence of L-selectin modulation on naïve T cells at these sites (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis in Figure 1A showing similar L-selectin expression on T cells in LN of NTB and 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: MDSC exclusion from LN is likely explained by their low L-selectin expression as compared to normal naïve T cells.
source: MDSC exclusion from LN is likely explained by their low L-selectin expression as compared to normal naïve T cells, (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric comparison in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing lower L-selectin expression on MDSC compared to naïve T cells.

claim: The uniformly high L-selectin density detected on intranodal T cells in both control and tumor-bearing mice is suggestive of a stringent requirement for a high L-selectin threshold for entry of blood-borne T cells across HEV.
source: The uniformly high L-selectin density detected on intranodal T cells in both control and tumor-bearing mice is suggestive of a stringent requirement for a high L-selectin threshold for entry of blood-borne T cells across HEV.
evidence: Based on inference from flow cytometric data showing consistently high L-selectin on intranodal T cells regardless of tumor status.

claim: Profound L-selectin downregulation was detected in naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the blood and splenic compartment of female and male 4T1-bearing mice.
source: In contrast, we detected profound L-selectin downregulation in naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells that was associated with substantial MDSC elevation in the blood and splenic compartment of female and male 4T1-bearing mice (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A showing reduced L-selectin MFI on splenic and blood T cells in 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: Splenic CD11b+Gr-1+ cells from 4T1-bearing mice exhibited prototypical MDSC suppressor function defined by potent inhibition of CD3/CD28-driven proliferation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells from non-tumor bearing mice in vitro.
source: Splenic CD11b+Gr-1+ cells from 4T1-bearing mice were confirmed to exhibit prototypical MDSC suppressor function defined by potent inhibition of CD3/CD28-driven proliferation of CD4+ and CD8+ T cells (from non-tumor bearing mice) in vitro (Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by T cell suppression assay data in Figure 1B showing dose-dependent suppression of T cell proliferation by MDSC.

claim: Control CD11b+ cells from non-tumor bearing mice were not immunosuppressive.
source: Conversely, control CD11b+ cells from non-tumor bearing mice were not immunosuppressive.
evidence: Supported by T cell suppression assay data in Figure 1B showing no suppression by NTB CD11b+ cells.

claim: There was an overall decrease in naïve T cells in LN and an increase in spleens of 4T1-bearing mice without changes in the apoptotic index.
source: Data showing an overall decrease in naïve T cells in LN, together with an increase in spleens of 4T1-bearing mice without changes in the apoptotic index (Figure 1C), support the notion that suboptimal L-selectin expression reduces T cell access to LN and causes compensatory redistribution to the spleen.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric quantification in Figure 1C showing total numbers of viable naïve T cells and percentages of annexin V+ cells in LN and spleens.

claim: Suboptimal L-selectin expression reduces T cell access to LN and causes compensatory redistribution to the spleen.
source: Data showing an overall decrease in naïve T cells in LN, together with an increase in spleens of 4T1-bearing mice without changes in the apoptotic index (Figure 1C), support the notion that suboptimal L-selectin expression reduces T cell access to LN and causes compensatory redistribution to the spleen.
evidence: Inference based on observed changes in T cell distribution between LN and spleen in tumor-bearing mice with reduced L-selectin.

claim: L-selectin loss on splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells correlated temporally with the extent of MDSC expansion in different murine tumor types.
source: We further determined that L-selectin loss on splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells correlated temporally with the extent of MDSC expansion which varied among different murine tumor types.
evidence: Supported by longitudinal flow cytometric data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and Figure 1—figure supplement 3 showing correlation between MDSC accumulation and L-selectin downregulation over time.

claim: MDSC expansion early during tumor progression (7 days post-4T1 implantation) coincided with significant L-selectin downregulation on naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets.
source: Thus, while MDSC expansion early during tumor progression (i.e., 7 days post-4T1 implantation) coincided with significant L-selectin downregulation on naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets, even greater L-selectin loss occurred at later time-points with higher 4T1 tumor burdens at subcutaneous sites or the mammary fat pad (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by time-course flow cytometric data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D showing L-selectin downregulation at day 7 post-tumor implantation.

claim: Greater L-selectin loss occurred at later time-points with higher 4T1 tumor burdens at subcutaneous sites or the mammary fat pad.
source: Thus, while MDSC expansion early during tumor progression (i.e., 7 days post-4T1 implantation) coincided with significant L-selectin downregulation on naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cell subsets, even greater L-selectin loss occurred at later time-points with higher 4T1 tumor burdens at subcutaneous sites or the mammary fat pad (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B–D).
evidence: Supported by time-course flow cytometric data in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B-D showing progressive L-selectin downregulation with increasing tumor burden.

claim: MDSC expansion was delayed in C57BL/6 mice implanted with AT-3 mammary tumor cells compared to the 4T1 system.
source: Compared to the 4T1 system, MDSC expansion was delayed in C57BL/6 mice implanted with AT-3 mammary tumor cells derived from genetically-engineered MMTV-PyMT/B6 transgenic mice (MTAG) (Waight et al., 2013), corresponding with moderate but significant L-selectin downregulation on naïve T cell subsets at ≥21 days post-tumor implantation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by time-course flow cytometric data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3A showing delayed MDSC accumulation in AT-3 model compared to 4T1, with citation to prior work.

claim: Moderate but significant L-selectin downregulation occurred on naïve T cell subsets at ≥21 days post-AT-3 tumor implantation.
source: Compared to the 4T1 system, MDSC expansion was delayed in C57BL/6 mice implanted with AT-3 mammary tumor cells derived from genetically-engineered MMTV-PyMT/B6 transgenic mice (MTAG) (Waight et al., 2013), corresponding with moderate but significant L-selectin downregulation on naïve T cell subsets at ≥21 days post-tumor implantation (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 1—figure supplement 3B showing L-selectin downregulation at day 21 and 28 post-AT-3 implantation.

claim: L-selectin downregulation occurred on splenic T cells in B16 melanoma and CT26 colorectal tumor models, but only in rare individual mice with abundant MDSC.
source: L-selectin downregulation also occurred on splenic T cells in other tumor models including B16 melanoma and CT26 colorectal tumor, but only in rare individual mice with abundant MDSC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), consistent with observations that these tumors do not typically induce MDSC expansion (Youn et al., 2008; Fisher et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 1—figure supplement 4 showing L-selectin downregulation only in mice with high MDSC burdens, with citations to prior literature on MDSC expansion in these models.

claim: B16 melanoma and CT26 colorectal tumors do not typically induce MDSC expansion.
source: L-selectin downregulation also occurred on splenic T cells in other tumor models including B16 melanoma and CT26 colorectal tumor, but only in rare individual mice with abundant MDSC (Figure 1—figure supplement 4), consistent with observations that these tumors do not typically induce MDSC expansion (Youn et al., 2008; Fisher et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Youn et al., 2008; Fisher et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2015) documenting MDSC expansion patterns in these tumor models.

claim: Immunohistological staining of the spleen revealed dense focal accumulations of Gr-1+ cells congregating with CD3+ T cells in the marginal zone that were sharply segregated from intrafollicular B220+ B cells in 4T1-bearing mice.
source: Clues about the spatial regulation of L-selectin emerged from immunohistological staining of the spleen that revealed dense focal accumulations of Gr-1+ cells congregating with CD3+ T cells in the marginal zone that were sharply segregated from intrafollicular B220+ B cells in 4T1-bearing mice (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence microscopy images in Figure 1D showing spatial distribution of Gr-1+, CD3+, and B220+ cells in spleen.

claim: Splenic B cells express relatively low L-selectin compared to T cells.
source: Additional insight into the MDSC mechanism of action came from profiling of splenic B cells that showed that while these cells express relatively low L-selectin compared to T cells as reported previously (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004), there was no change in L-selectin density on splenic B cells of tumor-bearing mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004) and flow cytometric data in Figure 1E.

claim: There was no change in L-selectin density on splenic B cells of 4T1 tumor-bearing mice.
source: Additional insight into the MDSC mechanism of action came from profiling of splenic B cells that showed that while these cells express relatively low L-selectin compared to T cells as reported previously (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004), there was no change in L-selectin density on splenic B cells of tumor-bearing mice (Figure 1E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 1E showing similar L-selectin MFI on splenic B220+ cells in NTB and 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: Differential regulation of L-selectin in splenic T and B cells suggests a model in which close physical contact with MDSC is a prerequisite for L-selectin loss.
source: This differential regulation of L-selectin in splenic T and B cells suggests a model in which close physical contact with MDSC is a prerequisite for L-selectin loss.
evidence: Inference based on observed differential L-selectin regulation in T cells (which co-localize with MDSC) versus B cells (which are segregated from MDSC) in spleen.

claim: 4T1 tumor growth was equivalent in sham and splenectomized mice at 21 days post-tumor implantation.
source: We validated that 4T1 tumor growth and MDSC expansion in the blood was equivalent in sham and splenectomized mice at 21 days post-tumor implantation (Figure 2B and C), offsetting any concern that splenectomy might reduce the circulating MDSC burden as reported for lung tumor models (Cortez-Retamozo et al., 2012; Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by tumor volume measurements in Figure 2B showing no significant difference between sham and splenectomized mice.

claim: MDSC expansion in the blood was equivalent in sham and splenectomized 4T1-bearing mice at 21 days post-tumor implantation.
source: We validated that 4T1 tumor growth and MDSC expansion in the blood was equivalent in sham and splenectomized mice at 21 days post-tumor implantation (Figure 2B and C), offsetting any concern that splenectomy might reduce the circulating MDSC burden as reported for lung tumor models (Cortez-Retamozo et al., 2012; Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 2C showing similar CD11b+Gr-1+ cell percentages in blood of sham and splenectomized 4T1-bearing mice, with citations to prior work on splenectomy effects.

claim: Splenectomy might reduce the circulating MDSC burden in lung tumor models.
source: We validated that 4T1 tumor growth and MDSC expansion in the blood was equivalent in sham and splenectomized mice at 21 days post-tumor implantation (Figure 2B and C), offsetting any concern that splenectomy might reduce the circulating MDSC burden as reported for lung tumor models (Cortez-Retamozo et al., 2012; Levy et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Cortez-Retamozo et al., 2012; Levy et al., 2015) reporting effects of splenectomy on MDSC burden in lung tumor models.

claim: High L-selectin expression was maintained following transfer of CD8+ T cells into sham, non-tumor bearing controls.
source: High L-selectin expression was maintained following transfer of CD8+ T cells (input cells) into sham, non-tumor bearing controls whereas substantial L-selectin loss occurred within a 24 hr window after transfer into sham-treated 4T1-bearing mice with high MDSC burdens (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 2C showing maintained L-selectin MFI on transferred CD8+ T cells in NTB recipients.

claim: Substantial L-selectin loss occurred within a 24 hr window after transfer of CD8+ T cells into sham-treated 4T1-bearing mice with high MDSC burdens.
source: High L-selectin expression was maintained following transfer of CD8+ T cells (input cells) into sham, non-tumor bearing controls whereas substantial L-selectin loss occurred within a 24 hr window after transfer into sham-treated 4T1-bearing mice with high MDSC burdens (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 2C showing reduced L-selectin MFI on transferred CD8+ T cells 24 hr post-ACT in 4T1-bearing recipients.

claim: The extent of L-selectin downregulation on adoptively-transferred CD8+ T cells was indistinguishable whether tumor-bearing recipient mice underwent sham surgery or splenectomy.
source: We surprisingly found that the extent of L-selectin downregulation on adoptively-transferred CD8+ T cells was indistinguishable whether tumor-bearing recipient mice underwent sham surgery or splenectomy.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 2C showing similar L-selectin downregulation on transferred CD8+ T cells in sham and splenectomized 4T1-bearing recipients.

claim: L-selectin down-modulation on CD8+ T cells can occur in the intravascular space and does not require structural scaffolds provided by organized tissue compartments.
source: These results suggested that L-selectin down-modulation on CD8+ T cells can occur in the intravascular space and does not require structural scaffolds provided by organized tissue compartments.
evidence: Inference based on observation that L-selectin downregulation occurs equally in splenectomized and sham-operated tumor-bearing mice.

claim: L-selectin was strongly downregulated on CD4+ T cells of tumor-bearing mice regardless of whether there was an intact splenic microenvironment.
source: Like CD8+ T cells, we found that L-selectin was strongly downregulated on CD4+ T cells of tumor-bearing mice regardless of whether there was an intact splenic microenvironment (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1 showing L-selectin downregulation on endogenous CD4+ T cells in both sham and splenectomized 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: L-selectin fluctuates after B cells exit the bone marrow and recirculate through the blood and spleen.
source: In the case of B220+ B cells, the varying levels of baseline L-selectin detected in lymphoid organs of tumor-free mice was expected since L-selectin is known to fluctuate after B cells exit the bone marrow and recirculate through the blood and spleen (Tang et al., 1998; Morrison et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 1998; Morrison et al., 2010) documenting L-selectin regulation on B cells.

claim: L-selectin was not downregulated in the bone marrow and splenic compartments of B cells despite increased MDSC burden in sham or splenectomized tumor-bearing mice.
source: Moreover, we did not detect L-selectin loss in the bone marrow and splenic compartments despite increased MDSC burden in sham or splenectomized tumor-bearing mice (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 3 showing similar L-selectin MFI on B220+ cells in bone marrow and spleen of NTB and 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: L-selectin was nearly completely downregulated on blood-borne B220+ B cells in both sham and splenectomized tumor-bearing mice.
source: In sharp contrast, L-selectin was nearly completely downregulated on blood-borne B220+ B cells in both sham and splenectomized tumor-bearing mice (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 3 showing markedly reduced L-selectin MFI on blood B220+ cells in both sham and splenectomized 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: The blood compartment is the preferential site of L-selectin modulation for B cells in tumor-bearing mice.
source: These observations allowed us to pinpoint the blood compartment as the preferential site of L-selectin modulation for B cells in tumor-bearing mice.
evidence: Inference based on observation that L-selectin downregulation on B cells occurs specifically in blood but not in bone marrow or spleen.

claim: Similar results for L-selectin downregulation on circulating T and B lymphocytes were obtained if the timing sequence was reversed by allowing tumor-induced MDSC to accrue prior to splenectomy.
source: Similar results were obtained for L-selectin downregulation on circulating T and B lymphocytes if the timing sequence was reversed by allowing tumor-induced MDSC to accrue prior to splenectomy (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1 showing L-selectin downregulation when splenectomy was performed after tumor establishment.

claim: Strong L-selectin downregulation occurred only 2 hr after adoptive transfer of naïve CD8+ and CD4+ T cells and B220+ B cells into the MDSC-rich vascular compartment of 4T1-bearing mice.
source: The conclusion that blood is a prominent site of L-selectin loss was further supported by the strong L-selectin downregulation observed only 2 hr after adoptive transfer of naïve CD8+ and CD4+ T cells and B220+ B cells into the MDSC-rich vascular compartment of 4T1-bearing mice (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing L-selectin downregulation on transferred lymphocytes 2 hr post-ACT.

claim: Labeled cells detected in the blood at 2 hr post-transfer mainly represent transferred populations retained in the vascular compartment since 2 hr is not sufficient for lymphocytes to recirculate from blood, through tissues, and back to the blood.
source: Labeled cells detected in the blood at this short time-point mainly represent transferred populations retained in the vascular compartment since 2 hr is not sufficient for lymphocytes to recirculate from blood, through tissues, and back to the blood (e.g., transit times for T cells through lymph nodes, spleen, and peripheral tissues are ~8–12, 5, and 24 hr, respectively, and ~24 hr for B cells at these tissue sites) (Ford, 1979; Issekutz et al., 1982; Girard et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Ford, 1979; Issekutz et al., 1982; Girard et al., 2012) documenting lymphocyte transit times through various tissues.

claim: Transit times for T cells through lymph nodes, spleen, and peripheral tissues are ~8–12, 5, and 24 hr, respectively.
source: Labeled cells detected in the blood at this short time-point mainly represent transferred populations retained in the vascular compartment since 2 hr is not sufficient for lymphocytes to recirculate from blood, through tissues, and back to the blood (e.g., transit times for T cells through lymph nodes, spleen, and peripheral tissues are ~8–12, 5, and 24 hr, respectively, and ~24 hr for B cells at these tissue sites) (Ford, 1979; Issekutz et al., 1982; Girard et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Ford, 1979; Issekutz et al., 1982; Girard et al., 2012) documenting lymphocyte transit times.

claim: Transit time for B cells through lymph nodes, spleen, and peripheral tissues is ~24 hr.
source: Labeled cells detected in the blood at this short time-point mainly represent transferred populations retained in the vascular compartment since 2 hr is not sufficient for lymphocytes to recirculate from blood, through tissues, and back to the blood (e.g., transit times for T cells through lymph nodes, spleen, and peripheral tissues are ~8–12, 5, and 24 hr, respectively, and ~24 hr for B cells at these tissue sites) (Ford, 1979; Issekutz et al., 1982; Girard et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Ford, 1979; Issekutz et al., 1982; Girard et al., 2012) documenting B cell transit times.

claim: Lymphocytes are the primary source of the circulating sL-selectin pool under normal conditions.
source: Lymphocytes are the primary source of the circulating sL-selectin pool under normal conditions, as demonstrated in studies showing that serum sL-selectin concentrations are reduced ~70% in lymphocyte-deficient Rag2−/− mice (Tu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Tu et al., 2002) demonstrating reduced sL-selectin in lymphocyte-deficient mice.

claim: Serum sL-selectin concentrations are reduced ~70% in lymphocyte-deficient Rag2−/− mice.
source: Lymphocytes are the primary source of the circulating sL-selectin pool under normal conditions, as demonstrated in studies showing that serum sL-selectin concentrations are reduced ~70% in lymphocyte-deficient Rag2−/− mice (Tu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Tu et al., 2002) documenting sL-selectin levels in Rag2−/− mice.

claim: Increased serum sL-selectin in tumor-bearing mice likely reflects MDSC-induced cleavage from lymphocyte surface membranes although MDSC could be an additional source of sL-selectin.
source: Thus, increased serum sL-selectin in tumor-bearing mice likely reflects MDSC-induced cleavage from lymphocyte surface membranes although MDSC could be an additional source of sL-selectin.
evidence: Inference based on observed correlation between MDSC expansion, lymphocyte L-selectin loss, and elevated serum sL-selectin.

claim: Elevated circulating sL-selectin at concentrations detected in tumor-bearing mice (1 µg/mL) functions as a competitive antagonist of L-selectin-directed lymphocyte homing in vivo.
source: Accordingly, two independent but complementary mechanisms are proposed to reduce LN trafficking in cancer: (1) MDSC-directed downregulation of lymphocyte L-selectin which we showed negatively impacts homing in HEV, and (2) elevated circulating sL-selectin which, at the concentrations detected in tumor-bearing mice (1 µg/mL in tumor-bearing mice compared to ~0.4 µg/mL in tumor-free controls), reportedly functions as a competitive antagonist of L-selectin-directed lymphocyte homing in vivo.
evidence: Inference based on measured sL-selectin concentrations in tumor-bearing mice and prior literature on sL-selectin antagonist function.

claim: Elevation of circulating sL-selectin levels in L-selectin−/− mice to ~0.9 and 1.5 μg/mL by serum infusion reduces lymphocyte trafficking to LN HEV by ~40% and 65%, respectively.
source: In this regard, elevation of circulating sL-selectin levels in L-selectin−/− mice to ~0.9 and 1.5 μg/mL by serum infusion reduces lymphocyte trafficking to LN HEV by ~40% and 65%, respectively, while concentrations of ~0.6 μg/mL are not inhibitory (Tu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Tu et al., 2002) documenting dose-dependent inhibition of lymphocyte homing by sL-selectin.

claim: sL-selectin concentrations of ~0.6 μg/mL are not inhibitory to lymphocyte trafficking to LN HEV.
source: In this regard, elevation of circulating sL-selectin levels in L-selectin−/− mice to ~0.9 and 1.5 μg/mL by serum infusion reduces lymphocyte trafficking to LN HEV by ~40% and 65%, respectively, while concentrations of ~0.6 μg/mL are not inhibitory (Tu et al., 2002).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Tu et al., 2002) documenting threshold for sL-selectin inhibition of homing.

claim: MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation does not depend on the main L-selectin sheddase, ADAM17, acting either in a cis or trans orientation.
source: Surprisingly, MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation does not depend on the main L-selectin sheddase, ADAM17, acting either in a cis or trans orientation.
evidence: Supported by experimental data using ADAM17 inhibitors, L(E)-selectin mutant mice, and Adam17−/− mice showing MDSC-induced L-selectin loss is ADAM17-independent.

claim: MDSC do not activate lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 to cleave L-selectin in cis.
source: In this regard, evidence that MDSC-induced L-selectin loss occurs in ADAM17-deficient lymphocytes indicates that MDSC do not activate lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 to cleave L-selectin in cis.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5D and 5E showing MDSC-induced L-selectin loss in Adam17−/− lymphocytes.

claim: ADAM17 present on the surface of MDSC does not act in trans to target L-selectin on juxtaposed lymphocyte membranes.
source: Nor does ADAM17 present on the surface of MDSC (Hanson et al., 2009; Oh et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2014) act in trans to target L-selectin on juxtaposed lymphocyte membranes since downregulation occurs in the presence of ADAM17-specific inhibitors and in cells expressing a mutated ADAM17 cleavage site (i.e., L(E)-selectin).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5D and 5E showing MDSC-induced L-selectin loss in presence of ADAM17 inhibitors and in L(E)-selectin cells, with citations to prior work documenting ADAM17 expression on MDSC.

claim: MDSC express surface ADAM17.
source: Nor does ADAM17 present on the surface of MDSC (Hanson et al., 2009; Oh et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2014) act in trans to target L-selectin on juxtaposed lymphocyte membranes since downregulation occurs in the presence of ADAM17-specific inhibitors and in cells expressing a mutated ADAM17 cleavage site (i.e., L(E)-selectin).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Hanson et al., 2009; Oh et al., 2013; Parker et al., 2014) documenting ADAM17 expression on MDSC.

claim: The mechanism underlying MDSC-induced L-selectin modulation closely parallels in vitro observations for an ADAM17 and ADAM10-independent ecto-protease during constitutive or inducible L-selectin shedding.
source: The mechanism underlying MDSC-induced L-selectin modulation closely parallels in vitro observations for an ADAM17 and ADAM10-independent ecto-protease during constitutive or inducible L-selectin shedding (i.e., triggered by antibody cross-linking of L-selectin and TcR) that is unaffected by mutation of the ADAM17 cleavage site, ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitors, or ADAM17-deficiency (Stoddart et al., 1996; Jasuja and Mier, 2000; Walcheck et al., 2003; Li et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Stoddart et al., 1996; Jasuja and Mier, 2000; Walcheck et al., 2003; Li et al., 2006) documenting ADAM17-independent L-selectin shedding mechanisms.

claim: Tumor-induced MDSC are enriched for multiple ecto-proteases including ADAM28, ADAM9, collagenase-3 (MMP13), stromelysin (MMP3), macrophage elastase, and leukocyte elastase.
source: Of note, tumor-induced MDSC are enriched for multiple ecto-proteases including ADAM28, ADAM9, collagenase-3 (MMP13), stromelysin (MMP3), macrophage elastase, and leukocyte elastase (Aliper et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Aliper et al., 2014) documenting ecto-protease expression in MDSC.

claim: Recombinant stromelysin (MMP3) can function in trans to cleave lymphocyte L-selectin in vitro.
source: Moreover, at least one of these proteins, recombinant stromelysin (MMP3), can function in trans to cleave lymphocyte L-selectin in vitro (Preece et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Preece et al., 1996) demonstrating MMP3-mediated L-selectin cleavage.

claim: B cells reportedly support MDSC development during cancer progression.
source: While B cells reportedly support MDSC development during cancer progression (Bodogai et al., 2015), to our knowledge this is the first demonstration that B cells are targets of tumor-induced MDSC.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Bodogai et al., 2015) documenting B cell support of MDSC development.

claim: This is the first demonstration that B cells are targets of tumor-induced MDSC.
source: While B cells reportedly support MDSC development during cancer progression (Bodogai et al., 2015), to our knowledge this is the first demonstration that B cells are targets of tumor-induced MDSC.
evidence: Claim of novelty based on authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: MDSC derived from mice with collagen-induced arthritis directly suppress B cell proliferation and antibody production in vitro.
source: These findings complement studies in autoimmunity showing that MDSC derived from mice with collagen-induced arthritis directly suppress B cell proliferation and antibody production in vitro (Crook et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Crook et al., 2015) documenting MDSC suppression of B cells in autoimmunity model.

claim: The nearly complete loss of L-selectin detected on circulating B cells in response to MDSC strongly suggests that B cell homing at HEV would be effectively blocked.
source: The nearly complete loss of L-selectin detected on circulating B cells in response to MDSC in our study strongly suggests that B cell homing at HEV would be effectively blocked, especially given the well-established sensitivity of B cells to perturbations in L-selectin density (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004).
evidence: Inference based on observed L-selectin loss on B cells and citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004) documenting B cell sensitivity to L-selectin levels.

claim: B cells are well-established to be sensitive to perturbations in L-selectin density.
source: The nearly complete loss of L-selectin detected on circulating B cells in response to MDSC in our study strongly suggests that B cell homing at HEV would be effectively blocked, especially given the well-established sensitivity of B cells to perturbations in L-selectin density (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004) documenting B cell sensitivity to L-selectin levels.

claim: Antibody responses would be expected to be severely diminished as a result of MDSC-induced suboptimal trafficking of both naïve B cells and CD4+ precursors of the follicular helper T cells required for T-dependent antibody production in LN.
source: Thus, antibody responses would be expected to be severely diminished as a result of MDSC-induced suboptimal trafficking of both naïve B cells and CD4+ precursors of the follicular helper T cells required for T-dependent antibody production in LN.
evidence: Inference based on observed L-selectin loss on B cells and CD4+ T cells and knowledge of requirements for antibody production.

claim: Patients diagnosed with premalignant advanced colonic adenomas who have elevated circulating MDSC failed to produce antibodies in response to vaccination with the MUC-1 tumor-associated antigen.
source: Collectively, our findings could provide an explanation for observations that patients diagnosed with premalignant advanced colonic adenomas who have elevated circulating MDSC failed to produce antibodies in response to vaccination with the MUC-1 tumor-associated antigen (Kimura et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Kimura et al., 2013) documenting failed antibody responses in patients with elevated MDSC.

claim: Adoptive transfer of activated L-selectin+CCR7+ stem cell memory T cells (TSCM) has greater antitumor efficacy than terminally differentiated L-selectinloCCR7lo cytolytic effectors.
source: This is founded on recent preclinical studies demonstrating that adoptive transfer of activated L-selectin+CCR7+ stem cell memory T cells (TSCM) has greater antitumor efficacy than terminally differentiated L-selectinloCCR7lo cytolytic effectors (Gattinoni et al., 2005, 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Gattinoni et al., 2005, 2011) demonstrating superior efficacy of TSCM in ACT therapy.

claim: The superior efficacy of TSCM is attributed to the requirement for adoptively-transferred cells to undergo L-selectin-dependent trafficking via HEV to access intranodal growth and survival factors.
source: The superior efficacy of TSCM is attributed to the requirement for adoptively-transferred cells to undergo L-selectin-dependent trafficking via HEV to access intranodal growth and survival factors (Gattinoni et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Gattinoni et al., 2005) explaining mechanism of TSCM efficacy.

claim: The efficacy of ACT therapy is limited by MDSC.
source: Of related interest are preclinical data showing that the efficacy of ACT therapy is limited by MDSC (Alizadeh et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Alizadeh et al., 2014) documenting MDSC limitation of ACT efficacy.

claim: An unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is that a high proportion of transferred T cells will undergo rapid L-selectin loss within 24 hr.
source: Our findings suggest that an unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is that a high proportion of transferred T cells will undergo two major MDSC-mediated events that impair T cell responses in LN: (1) reduced LN homing due to rapid L-selectin loss within 24 hr, and (2) immune suppression stemming from T cell preconditioning prior to direct tumor-antigen exposure.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing rapid L-selectin loss on transferred T cells in MDSC-rich environment.

claim: An unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is immune suppression stemming from T cell preconditioning prior to direct tumor-antigen exposure.
source: Our findings suggest that an unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is that a high proportion of transferred T cells will undergo two major MDSC-mediated events that impair T cell responses in LN: (1) reduced LN homing due to rapid L-selectin loss within 24 hr, and (2) immune suppression stemming from T cell preconditioning prior to direct tumor-antigen exposure.
evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing MDSC preconditioning reduces T cell responsiveness to antigen.

claim: These MDSC-mediated mechanisms would necessitate the transfer of excessive numbers of ex vivo-expanded T cells to achieve therapeutic efficacy in ACT therapy.
source: These mechanisms would necessitate the transfer of excessive numbers of ex vivo-expanded T cells to achieve therapeutic efficacy.
evidence: Inference based on observed MDSC-mediated impairment of transferred T cell function.

claim: L-selectin loss is not indelibly imprinted on T cells.
source: Findings that L-selectin loss is not indelibly imprinted on T cells suggest that neoadjuvant treatments that target MDSC could offer promise for immune-based cancer therapies that depend on T and B cell trafficking to lymph nodes.
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing L-selectin recovery on T cells after MDSC depletion.

claim: Neoadjuvant treatments that target MDSC could offer promise for immune-based cancer therapies that depend on T and B cell trafficking to lymph nodes.
source: Findings that L-selectin loss is not indelibly imprinted on T cells suggest that neoadjuvant treatments that target MDSC could offer promise for immune-based cancer therapies that depend on T and B cell trafficking to lymph nodes.
evidence: Inference based on reversibility of L-selectin loss after MDSC removal.

claim: Tumor-induced MDSC act from remote sites through two independent mechanisms to suppress systemic adaptive immunity in widely dispersed LN.
source: Here we provide evidence that tumor-induced MDSC act from remote sites through two independent mechanisms to suppress systemic adaptive immunity in widely dispersed LN.
evidence: Summary claim based on multiple experimental findings throughout the study.

claim: MDSC located in anatomically discrete sub-compartments of the spleen and blood downregulate expression of the L-selectin LN homing receptor in murine CD4+ and CD8+ naïve T cell subsets and on blood-borne murine B cells.
source: The major findings of the current study establish that MDSC located in anatomically discrete sub-compartments of the spleen and, unexpectedly in the blood, downregulate expression of the L-selectin LN homing receptor in murine CD4+ and CD8+ naïve T cell subsets and on blood-borne murine B cells.
evidence: Summary claim based on flow cytometric data and splenectomy experiments throughout the study.

claim: Even moderate L-selectin loss severely limits trafficking of naïve CD8+ T cells across HEV.
source: In the case of naïve CD8+ T cells, even moderate L-selectin loss severely limits trafficking across HEV, causing a profound reduction in antigen-driven expansion within the LN stroma.
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data in Figure 6 and competitive homing assays in Figure 7.

claim: Moderate L-selectin loss causes a profound reduction in antigen-driven expansion of CD8+ T cells within the LN stroma.
source: In the case of naïve CD8+ T cells, even moderate L-selectin loss severely limits trafficking across HEV, causing a profound reduction in antigen-driven expansion within the LN stroma.
evidence: Supported by competitive activation assay data in Figure 8 showing ~70:1 ratio of activated L-selectinhi vs L-selectinint/lo OT-I cells in draining LN.

claim: MDSC-induced L-selectin down-modulation could significantly impair immune surveillance during the early phases of tumor escape.
source: Thus, MDSC-induced L-selectin down-modulation could significantly impair immune surveillance during the early phases of tumor escape as well as compromise immunotherapy regimens dependent on immune cell access to LN.
evidence: Inference based on observed L-selectin downregulation early in tumor progression and its impact on trafficking.

claim: MDSC-induced L-selectin down-modulation could compromise immunotherapy regimens dependent on immune cell access to LN.
source: Thus, MDSC-induced L-selectin down-modulation could significantly impair immune surveillance during the early phases of tumor escape as well as compromise immunotherapy regimens dependent on immune cell access to LN.
evidence: Inference based on observed impact of L-selectin loss on T cell trafficking and function.

claim: T cells can be preconditioned by MDSC in the spleen or blood, resulting in diminished responsiveness to subsequent challenge with cognate antigen.
source: Additionally, our results reveal that T cells can be preconditioned by MDSC in the spleen or blood, resulting in diminished responsiveness to subsequent challenge with cognate antigen.
evidence: Supported by in vitro preconditioning assays in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 and in vivo competitive activation assays in Figure 8.

claim: LN are important sites of MDSC suppression which could not be predicted from routine profiling of immune constituents since MDSC are largely excluded from this lymphoid compartment.
source: Collectively, these findings lead us to propose that LN are important sites of MDSC suppression which could not be predicted from routine profiling of immune constituents since MDSC are largely excluded from this lymphoid compartment.
evidence: Inference based on observed MDSC exclusion from LN yet profound impact on intranodal T cell responses.

claim: The spleen is a major reservoir for peripheral MDSC with direct immunosuppressive activity.
source: The spleen is already considered a major reservoir for peripheral MDSC with direct immunosuppressive activity (Gabrilovich et al., 2012), while the blood is not known to be an active site of MDSC function in situ.
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Gabrilovich et al., 2012) documenting splenic MDSC function.

claim: The blood is not known to be an active site of MDSC function in situ.
source: The spleen is already considered a major reservoir for peripheral MDSC with direct immunosuppressive activity (Gabrilovich et al., 2012), while the blood is not known to be an active site of MDSC function in situ.
evidence: Statement of prior knowledge in the field before the current study.

claim: MDSC are discretely compartmentalized within the splenic marginal zone of tumor-bearing mice.
source: In line with prior studies (Ugel et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2012), we found discrete compartmentalization of MDSC within the splenic marginal zone of tumor-bearing mice.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1D and citations to prior literature (Ugel et al., 2012; Zhao et al., 2012).

claim: MDSC localization in the splenic marginal zone was linked to specific downregulation of L-selectin on T cells but not B cells, consistent with MDSC exclusion from B cell follicles.
source: This localization was linked to specific downregulation of L-selectin on T cells but not B cells, consistent with MDSC exclusion from B cell follicles.
evidence: Supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1D showing spatial segregation and flow cytometric data in Figure 1E showing differential L-selectin regulation.

claim: The blood is a major site for MDSC-targeted L-selectin downregulation for both T and B cells.
source: However, subsequent analysis of splenectomized tumor-bearing mice revealed that the blood is a major site for MDSC-targeted L-selectin downregulation for both T and B cells.
evidence: Supported by splenectomy experiments in Figures 2 and 3 showing L-selectin downregulation occurs independently of spleen.

claim: MDSC-to-target cell contact is a prerequisite for L-selectin down-modulation.
source: Evidence that L-selectin down-modulation is restricted to specific organs as well as sub-anatomical compartments supports a scenario in which MDSC-to-target cell contact is a prerequisite for L-selectin down-modulation, as validated by MDSC-lymphocyte co-cultures in the present study.
evidence: Supported by transwell co-culture experiments in Figure 4D showing contact-dependence.

claim: Biological consequences occur as a result of cell-to-cell interactions within the blood.
source: There is precedent from other systems that biological consequences occur as a result of cell-to-cell interactions within the blood, suggesting that MDSC could also be expected to have contact-dependent intravascular activities.
evidence: General statement about precedent in other biological systems used to support plausibility of MDSC function in blood.

claim: Leukocyte-leukocyte interactions along vessel walls contribute to recruitment at inflammatory sites.
source: In this regard, leukocyte-leukocyte interactions along vessel walls contribute to recruitment at inflammatory sites (Grailer et al., 2009) while stable aggregates comprised of circulating tumor cells and other cell types (e.g., leukocytes, platelets, stromal cells) function as 'traveling niches' to facilitate metastasis (Krebs et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Grailer et al., 2009) documenting leukocyte-leukocyte interactions in inflammation.

claim: Stable aggregates comprised of circulating tumor cells and other cell types function as 'traveling niches' to facilitate metastasis.
source: In this regard, leukocyte-leukocyte interactions along vessel walls contribute to recruitment at inflammatory sites (Grailer et al., 2009) while stable aggregates comprised of circulating tumor cells and other cell types (e.g., leukocytes, platelets, stromal cells) function as 'traveling niches' to facilitate metastasis (Krebs et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Krebs et al., 2014) documenting traveling niches in metastasis.

claim: Human MDSC comprise up to 45% of PBMC in cancer patients.
source: Thus, the high circulating MDSC concentration in tumor-bearing mice shown in the current report and in cancer patients (e.g., human MDSC comprise up to 45% of PBMC) (Trellakis et al., 2013) makes serial contact with target lymphocytes plausible either in free-flowing blood, within multicellular aggregates, or in marginated pools within capillaries, sinusoids or intravascular niches in the lung where naïve lymphocytes are transiently retained (Galkina et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Trellakis et al., 2013) documenting MDSC frequencies in cancer patients.

claim: Naïve lymphocytes are transiently retained in intravascular niches in the lung.
source: Thus, the high circulating MDSC concentration in tumor-bearing mice shown in the current report and in cancer patients (e.g., human MDSC comprise up to 45% of PBMC) (Trellakis et al., 2013) makes serial contact with target lymphocytes plausible either in free-flowing blood, within multicellular aggregates, or in marginated pools within capillaries, sinusoids or intravascular niches in the lung where naïve lymphocytes are transiently retained (Galkina et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Galkina et al., 2005) documenting lymphocyte retention in lung.

claim: L-selectin status is a critical determinant of homing potential since lymphocytes emigrating from spleen or blood have nearly immediate access to LN HEV.
source: Regardless of whether the loss occurs in spleen or blood, L-selectin status is a critical determinant of homing potential since lymphocytes emigrating from each of these sites have nearly immediate access to LN HEV (Chen et al., 2006).
evidence: Inference based on lymphocyte recirculation patterns, supported by citation to prior literature (Chen et al., 2006).

claim: The extent of the homing defect in HEV is remarkable considering the modest change in overall L-selectin surface density observed for T cells in the AT-3 tumor model.
source: The extent of the homing defect in HEV is remarkable considering the modest change in overall L-selectin surface density observed for T cells in the AT-3 tumor model.
evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings comparing magnitude of L-selectin loss to magnitude of homing defect.

claim: During leukocyte rolling it is estimated that ~5 microvillous tips are in simultaneous contact with endothelial surfaces, with L-selectin concentration exceeding 90,000 molecules per μm2 at a single microvillous tip.
source: During leukocyte rolling it is estimated that ~5 microvillous tips are in simultaneous contact with endothelial surfaces, with L-selectin concentration exceeding 90,000 molecules per μm2 at a single microvillous tip (Shao and Hochmuth, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Shao and Hochmuth, 1999) documenting L-selectin distribution during rolling.

claim: Relatively subtle decreases in L-selectin density within multivalent focal patches increase rolling speed, thus destabilizing adhesion within HEV.
source: Our results suggest that relatively subtle decreases in L-selectin density within these multivalent focal patches increase rolling speed, thus destabilizing adhesion within HEV.
evidence: Inference based on intravital microscopy data in Figure 6 showing increased rolling velocity with moderate L-selectin loss.

claim: Intermediate L-selectin downregulation in genetically engineered L-selectin+/− T cells causes diminished rolling quality.
source: These data are reminiscent of similar observations for diminished rolling quality due to intermediate L-selectin downregulation in genetically engineered L-selectin+/− T cells (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004) documenting rolling defects in L-selectin+/− cells.

claim: L-selectin modulation by MDSC is of primary importance during adhesion on the lumenal surface of HEV prior to extravasation.
source: Our intravital data demonstrate that L-selectin modulation by MDSC is of primary importance during adhesion on the lumenal surface of HEV prior to extravasation.
evidence: Interpretation of intravital microscopy data in Figure 6 showing defects in rolling and sticking.

claim: MDSC-mediated L-selectin loss may have downstream consequences in controlling the polarity of monocytes necessary for transendothelial migration.
source: These findings do not, however, exclude the possibility that MDSC-mediated L-selectin loss also has downstream consequences in light of in vitro studies implicating extended roles for L-selectin in controlling the polarity of monocytes necessary for transendothelial migration (Rzeniewicz et al., 2015) as well as antigen-driven acquisition of cytolytic function by CD8+ T cells (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Speculation based on citations to prior literature (Rzeniewicz et al., 2015; Yang et al., 2011) documenting additional L-selectin functions.

claim: L-selectin has extended roles in antigen-driven acquisition of cytolytic function by CD8+ T cells.
source: These findings do not, however, exclude the possibility that MDSC-mediated L-selectin loss also has downstream consequences in light of in vitro studies implicating extended roles for L-selectin in controlling the polarity of monocytes necessary for transendothelial migration (Rzeniewicz et al., 2015) as well as antigen-driven acquisition of cytolytic function by CD8+ T cells (Yang et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Yang et al., 2011) documenting L-selectin role in CD8+ T cell function.

claim: There is an unprecedented correlation between MDSC expansion, L-selectin loss by T and B lymphocytes, and a >2 fold increase in circulating sL-selectin in tumor-bearing mice.
source: The current results establish an unprecedented correlation between MDSC expansion, L-selectin loss by T and B lymphocytes, and a >2 fold increase in circulating sL-selectin in tumor-bearing mice.
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 5B showing elevated serum sL-selectin in 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: Serum sL-selectin levels are increased in patients with solid tumors (bladder and thyroid cancer).
source: Emerging clinical studies have reported that serum sL-selectin levels are also increased in patients with solid tumors (i.e., bladder and thyroid cancer), although links to MDSC were not explored (Choudhary et al., 2015; Kobawala et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Choudhary et al., 2015; Kobawala et al., 2016) documenting elevated sL-selectin in cancer patients.

claim: Partial MDSC depletion (~50%) by administration of anti-Gr-1 antibody at three day intervals after 4T1 implantation had no impact on tumor growth but significantly rescued L-selectin on circulating naïve T and B cells.
source: Partial MDSC depletion (~50%) by administration of anti-Gr-1 antibody at three day intervals after 4T1 implantation had no impact on tumor growth but significantly rescued L-selectin on circulating naïve T and B cells (Figure 4A and B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4A and B showing tumor volumes and L-selectin expression after anti-Gr-1 treatment.

claim: Complete L-selectin recovery occurred on CD4+ and CD8+ T cells within four days after culture or post-adoptive transfer into non-tumor bearing recipient mice when CD11b+ MDSC were depleted from L-selectinlo splenic populations from 4T1-bearing mice.
source: Complementary studies showed that L-selectin loss was reversible in an environment devoid of MDSC. In this regard, when CD11b+ MDSC were depleted from L-selectinlo splenic populations from 4T1-bearing mice we observed complete L-selectin recovery on CD4+ and CD8+ T cells within four days after culture or post-adoptive transfer into non-tumor bearing recipient mice (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing L-selectin recovery after MDSC depletion.

claim: Continued exposure to MDSC is required to maintain L-selectin down-modulation.
source: Thus, these findings demonstrate that continued exposure to MDSC is required to maintain L-selectin down-modulation.
evidence: Inference based on L-selectin recovery experiments in Figure 4C showing restoration after MDSC removal.

claim: Stronger L-selectin loss occurred if IFN-γ and LPS were included in MDSC-T cell co-cultures to sustain MDSC function ex vivo.
source: Stronger L-selectin loss occurred if IFN-γ and LPS were included in co-cultures to sustain MDSC function ex vivo (Sinha et al., 2007; Stewart et al., 2009; Ostrand-Rosenberg et al., 2012; Beury et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by in vitro co-culture data in Figure 4D and citations to prior literature (Sinha et al., 2007; Stewart et al., 2009; Ostrand-Rosenberg et al., 2012; Beury et al., 2014) documenting IFN-γ/LPS effects on MDSC function.

claim: MDSC acted through a contact-dependent mechanism that was abrogated if MDSC were physically separated from target lymphocytes by cell-impermeable transwell inserts.
source: Moreover, MDSC acted through a contact-dependent mechanism that was abrogated if MDSC were physically separated from target lymphocytes by cell-impermeable transwell inserts (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by transwell co-culture data in Figure 4D showing no L-selectin loss when MDSC and T cells are separated.

claim: MDSC directly target lymphocytes for L-selectin loss.
source: Taken together, these results establish that MDSC directly target lymphocytes for L-selectin loss.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches including MDSC depletion, co-culture, and transwell experiments.

claim: L-selectin mRNA levels were unchanged in splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells of 4T1-bearing mice compared to non-tumor bearing controls.
source: Further investigation into the mechanisms underlying MDSC activity showed that L-selectin mRNA levels detected by quantitative RT-PCR were unchanged in splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells of 4T1-bearing mice compared to non-tumor bearing controls (Figure 5A), indicating that L-selectin loss does not involve transcriptional repression in vivo.
evidence: Supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5A showing no change in L-selectin mRNA expression.

claim: L-selectin loss does not involve transcriptional repression in vivo.
source: Further investigation into the mechanisms underlying MDSC activity showed that L-selectin mRNA levels detected by quantitative RT-PCR were unchanged in splenic CD4+ and CD8+ T cells of 4T1-bearing mice compared to non-tumor bearing controls (Figure 5A), indicating that L-selectin loss does not involve transcriptional repression in vivo.
evidence: Inference based on qRT-PCR data showing unchanged mRNA levels despite reduced protein expression.

claim: MDSC-mediated L-selectin downmodulation was accompanied by a 2.5-fold increase in soluble (s)L-selectin in the serum.
source: MDSC-mediated L-selectin downmodulation was instead accompanied by a 2.5-fold increase in soluble (s)L-selectin in the serum which was in line with a sheddase-dependent mechanism operative in vivo (Figure 5B).
evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 5B showing elevated serum sL-selectin in 4T1-bearing mice.

claim: The 2.5-fold increase in soluble L-selectin in serum of tumor-bearing mice is in line with a sheddase-dependent mechanism operative in vivo.
source: MDSC-mediated L-selectin downmodulation was instead accompanied by a 2.5-fold increase in soluble (s)L-selectin in the serum which was in line with a sheddase-dependent mechanism operative in vivo (Figure 5B).
evidence: Inference based on observed elevation of sL-selectin consistent with proteolytic cleavage.

claim: L-selectin is a well-known target of the ADAM17 ecto-protease which operates in cis to cleave substrates on the same membrane surface.
source: L-selectin is a well-known target of the ADAM17 ecto-protease which operates in cis to cleave substrates on the same membrane surface (Feehan et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Feehan et al., 1996) documenting ADAM17-mediated L-selectin cleavage.

claim: PMA-induced L-selectin loss was abrogated by an ADAM17-specific inhibitor (PF-5480090).
source: Thus, in agreement with the obligate role of ADAM17 reported for PMA-induced L-selectin shedding, we found that PMA-induced loss of lymphocyte L-selectin was abrogated (1) by an ADAM17-specific inhibitor (PF-5480090) (McGowan et al., 2013) and by a dual ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitor (INCB7839) (Witters et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013); (2) in cells from L(E)-selectin mice expressing a mutated ADAM cleavage site due to substitution of the L-selectin membrane-proximal extracellular domain with the shorter E-selectin homologous domain (Venturi et al., 2003); or (3) in ADAM17-deficient lymphocytes from Adam17flox/flox/Vav1-Cre mice (Mishra et al., 2016) cultured alone (Figure 5C) or co-mixed with wildtype cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5C and citations to prior literature (McGowan et al., 2013) documenting PF-5480090 specificity.

claim: PMA-induced L-selectin loss was abrogated by a dual ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitor (INCB7839).
source: Thus, in agreement with the obligate role of ADAM17 reported for PMA-induced L-selectin shedding, we found that PMA-induced loss of lymphocyte L-selectin was abrogated (1) by an ADAM17-specific inhibitor (PF-5480090) (McGowan et al., 2013) and by a dual ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitor (INCB7839) (Witters et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013); (2) in cells from L(E)-selectin mice expressing a mutated ADAM cleavage site due to substitution of the L-selectin membrane-proximal extracellular domain with the shorter E-selectin homologous domain (Venturi et al., 2003); or (3) in ADAM17-deficient lymphocytes from Adam17flox/flox/Vav1-Cre mice (Mishra et al., 2016) cultured alone (Figure 5C) or co-mixed with wildtype cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5C and citations to prior literature (Witters et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013) documenting INCB7839 specificity.

claim: PMA-induced L-selectin loss was abrogated in cells from L(E)-selectin mice expressing a mutated ADAM cleavage site.
source: Thus, in agreement with the obligate role of ADAM17 reported for PMA-induced L-selectin shedding, we found that PMA-induced loss of lymphocyte L-selectin was abrogated (1) by an ADAM17-specific inhibitor (PF-5480090) (McGowan et al., 2013) and by a dual ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitor (INCB7839) (Witters et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013); (2) in cells from L(E)-selectin mice expressing a mutated ADAM cleavage site due to substitution of the L-selectin membrane-proximal extracellular domain with the shorter E-selectin homologous domain (Venturi et al., 2003); or (3) in ADAM17-deficient lymphocytes from Adam17flox/flox/Vav1-Cre mice (Mishra et al., 2016) cultured alone (Figure 5C) or co-mixed with wildtype cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5C and citation to prior literature (Venturi et al., 2003) describing L(E)-selectin mice.

claim: PMA-induced L-selectin loss was abrogated in ADAM17-deficient lymphocytes from Adam17flox/flox/Vav1-Cre mice.
source: Thus, in agreement with the obligate role of ADAM17 reported for PMA-induced L-selectin shedding, we found that PMA-induced loss of lymphocyte L-selectin was abrogated (1) by an ADAM17-specific inhibitor (PF-5480090) (McGowan et al., 2013) and by a dual ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitor (INCB7839) (Witters et al., 2008; Wang et al., 2013); (2) in cells from L(E)-selectin mice expressing a mutated ADAM cleavage site due to substitution of the L-selectin membrane-proximal extracellular domain with the shorter E-selectin homologous domain (Venturi et al., 2003); or (3) in ADAM17-deficient lymphocytes from Adam17flox/flox/Vav1-Cre mice (Mishra et al., 2016) cultured alone (Figure 5C) or co-mixed with wildtype cells (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1, and citation to prior literature (Mishra et al., 2016) describing Adam17−/− mice.

claim: There is a strict requirement for cis-acting ADAM17 for PMA-induced L-selectin down-modulation.
source: These findings confirm reports of a strict requirement for cis-acting ADAM17 for PMA-induced L-selectin down-modulation (Feehan et al., 1996; Preece et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by experimental data and citations to prior literature (Feehan et al., 1996; Preece et al., 1996) documenting cis-acting ADAM17 requirement.

claim: MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in vitro was unaffected by inhibitors of ADAM17 or ADAM17/ADAM10.
source: In contrast, MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in vitro was unaffected by inhibitors of ADAM17 or ADAM17/ADAM10; L(E)-selectin mutation; or lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 deficiency (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro co-culture data in Figure 5D showing L-selectin loss despite ADAM17 inhibition.

claim: MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in vitro was unaffected by L(E)-selectin mutation.
source: In contrast, MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in vitro was unaffected by inhibitors of ADAM17 or ADAM17/ADAM10; L(E)-selectin mutation; or lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 deficiency (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro co-culture data in Figure 5D showing L-selectin loss in L(E)-selectin cells.

claim: MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in vitro was unaffected by lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 deficiency.
source: In contrast, MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in vitro was unaffected by inhibitors of ADAM17 or ADAM17/ADAM10; L(E)-selectin mutation; or lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 deficiency (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by in vitro co-culture data in Figure 5D showing L-selectin loss in Adam17−/− cells.

claim: Elevated constitutive L-selectin expression in mutant L(E)-selectin lymphocytes or on Adam17−/− cells was indicative of an ADAM17 mechanism operative in vivo.
source: Further, while elevated constitutive L-selectin expression in mutant L(E)-selectin lymphocytes or on Adam17−/− cells was indicative of an ADAM17 mechanism operative in vivo as described previously (Venturi et al., 2003; Li et al., 2006), this pathway was dispensable for MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in mutant L(E)-selectin-expressing T and B cells or in Adam17−/− cells following their adoptive transfer into MDSChi 4T1-bearing SCID mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 5E and citations to prior literature (Venturi et al., 2003; Li et al., 2006) documenting elevated baseline L-selectin in these mutants.

claim: ADAM17 pathway was dispensable for MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in mutant L(E)-selectin-expressing T and B cells or in Adam17−/− cells following their adoptive transfer into MDSChi 4T1-bearing SCID mice.
source: Further, while elevated constitutive L-selectin expression in mutant L(E)-selectin lymphocytes or on Adam17−/− cells was indicative of an ADAM17 mechanism operative in vivo as described previously (Venturi et al., 2003; Li et al., 2006), this pathway was dispensable for MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation in mutant L(E)-selectin-expressing T and B cells or in Adam17−/− cells following their adoptive transfer into MDSChi 4T1-bearing SCID mice (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by adoptive transfer data in Figure 5E showing L-selectin loss in L(E)-selectin and Adam17−/− cells in tumor-bearing mice.

claim: These data exclude a role for ADAM17 or ADAM10 in either a cis or trans orientation for MDSC-induced L-selectin loss.
source: Collectively, these data exclude a role for ADAM17 or ADAM10 in either a cis or trans orientation for MDSC-induced L-selectin loss and are suggestive of the involvement of another ecto-protease.
evidence: Conclusion based on multiple experimental approaches using inhibitors, mutant mice, and knockout mice.

claim: The data are suggestive of the involvement of another ecto-protease in MDSC-induced L-selectin loss.
source: Collectively, these data exclude a role for ADAM17 or ADAM10 in either a cis or trans orientation for MDSC-induced L-selectin loss and are suggestive of the involvement of another ecto-protease.
evidence: Inference based on exclusion of ADAM17/ADAM10 yet observation of proteolytic cleavage.

claim: L-selectinint/loCD8+ T cells from AT-3-bearing mice exhibited a normal frequency of tethering and rolling interactions in HEV.
source: L-selectinint/loCD8+ T cells from AT-3-bearing mice surprisingly exhibited a normal frequency of tethering and rolling interactions in HEV (Figure 6C; Video 2).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data in Figure 6C showing similar rolling fractions for NTB and AT-3 CD8+ T cells.

claim: L-selectinint/loCD8+ T cells from AT-3-bearing mice exhibited a significant decrease in their transition from rolling to firm arrest in order IV and V venules.
source: However, we detected a significant decrease in their transition from rolling to firm arrest in order IV and V venules (Figure 6C; Video 2) despite normal expression and function of CCR7 and LFA-1, as determined by flow cytometric profiling, CCL21-driven chemotaxis assays, and LFA-1–dependent homotypic aggregation assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy data in Figure 6C showing reduced sticking fractions for AT-3 CD8+ T cells.

claim: L-selectinint/loCD8+ T cells from AT-3-bearing mice had normal expression and function of CCR7 and LFA-1.
source: However, we detected a significant decrease in their transition from rolling to firm arrest in order IV and V venules (Figure 6C; Video 2) despite normal expression and function of CCR7 and LFA-1, as determined by flow cytometric profiling, CCL21-driven chemotaxis assays, and LFA-1–dependent homotypic aggregation assays (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometry, chemotaxis, and aggregation assay data in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: L-selectinint/lo CD8+ T cells exhibited significantly faster median rolling velocity when compared to L-selectinhi CD8+ T cells in order V venular segments (65.0 versus 37.2 μm/sec, respectively).
source: An explanation for these paradoxical findings was revealed by data showing defective rolling behavior of L-selectinint/lo CD8+ T cells, as evidenced by their significantly faster median rolling velocity when compared to L-selectinhi CD8+ T cells in order V venular segments (65.0 versus 37.2 μm/sec, respectively; Figure 6D and E).
evidence: Supported by intravital microscopy rolling velocity measurements in Figure 6D and E.

claim: Homeostatic trafficking of L-selectinint/lo CD8+ T cells across LN HEV was strongly inhibited (~80%) when compared to L-selectinhi T cells.
source: Homeostatic trafficking of L-selectinint/lo CD8+ T cells across LN HEV was strongly inhibited (~80%) when compared to L-selectinhi T cells (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by competitive homing assay data in Figure 7A showing reduced homing of AT-3 CD8+ T cells to LN.

claim: Transferred CD8+ T cells that successfully extravasated across LN HEV during homeostatic trafficking were uniformly L-selectinhi regardless of whether they originated from non-tumor bearing mice or AT-3–bearing mice.
source: Transferred CD8+ T cells that successfully extravasated across LN HEV during homeostatic trafficking were uniformly L-selectinhi regardless of whether they originated from non-tumor bearing mice or AT-3–bearing mice (Figure 7B), suggesting that a high L-selectin density is necessary to stabilize T cell adhesion during extravasation.
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis in Figure 7B showing L-selectinhi phenotype on T cells recovered from LN.

claim: A high L-selectin density is necessary to stabilize T cell adhesion during extravasation across LN HEV.
source: Transferred CD8+ T cells that successfully extravasated across LN HEV during homeostatic trafficking were uniformly L-selectinhi regardless of whether they originated from non-tumor bearing mice or AT-3–bearing mice (Figure 7B), suggesting that a high L-selectin density is necessary to stabilize T cell adhesion during extravasation.
evidence: Inference based on observation that only L-selectinhi cells successfully home to LN.

claim: Differential L-selectin expression was maintained on transferred CD8+ T cells recovered from the spleen where trafficking is not dictated by L-selectin status.
source: In contrast, differential L-selectin expression was maintained on transferred CD8+ T cells recovered from the spleen where trafficking is not dictated by L-selectin status (Figure 7A and B).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 7B showing maintained L-selectin differences on T cells recovered from spleen.

claim: Reduced CD8+ T cell trafficking due to moderate L-selectin loss was also observed in an inflammatory model in which HEV express elevated CCL21 and ICAM-1 in response to fever-range whole body hyperthermia (WBH).
source: Reduced CD8+ T cell trafficking due to moderate L-selectin loss was also observed in an inflammatory model in which HEV express elevated CCL21 and ICAM-1 in response to fever-range whole body hyperthermia (WBH) (Figure 7A; Figure 7–figure supplement 1) (Chen et al., 2006; Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by competitive homing data in Figure 7A and immunofluorescence data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1, with citations to prior literature (Chen et al., 2006; Evans et al., 2015).

claim: Even moderate MDSC-induced L-selectin loss is sufficient to profoundly reduce homing and antigen-dependent activation of naïve CD8+ T cells in LN.
source: These results establish the biological significance of MDSC-induced L-selectin loss in limiting T cell access to LN via HEV portals.
evidence: Conclusion based on intravital microscopy and competitive homing data showing functional consequences of moderate L-selectin loss.

claim: OT-I T cells from non-tumor bearing mice were ≥2 times more responsive to antigen-driven proliferation than OT-I cells from AT-3-bearing mice in vitro.
source: Co-cultures of OT-I cells from non-tumor bearing mice and AT-3–bearing transgenic mice (i.e., 1:1 ratio) were stimulated in vitro for four days with SIINFEKL-loaded bone marrow-derived dendritic cells (DC). OT-I T cells from non-tumor bearing mice were ≥2 times more responsive to antigen-driven proliferation than OT-I cells from AT-3-bearing mice (Figure 8B and C).
evidence: Supported by in vitro competitive activation assay data in Figure 8B showing differential proliferation.

claim: Transient co-culture of MDSC with naïve OT-I CD8+ or DO11.10 CD4+ TcR-transgenic cells (16 hr 'preconditioning' phase), followed by removal of MDSC, markedly suppressed T cell proliferation during subsequent challenge with cognate peptide antigens.
source: These studies revealed that transient co-culture of MDSC with naïve OT-I CD8+ or DO11.10 CD4+ TcR-transgenic cells (i.e., 16 hr 'preconditioning' phase), followed by removal of MDSC, markedly suppressed T cell proliferation during subsequent challenge with cognate peptide antigens (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by preconditioning assay data in Figure 8—figure supplement 1B showing suppressed proliferation after MDSC preconditioning.

claim: Activated OT-I T cells from tumor-free donors outnumbered OT-I cells from AT-3–bearing donors by ~70:1 in draining popliteal LN four days after adoptive transfer into vaccinated non-tumor bearing recipients.
source: Flow cytometric analysis of transferred cells recovered from the draining popliteal LN (dLN) four days after adoptive transfer revealed that activated OT-I T cells from tumor-free donors outnumbered OT-I cells from AT-3–bearing donors by ~70:1 (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by in vivo competitive activation assay data in Figure 8C showing dramatic bias toward NTB OT-I cells in dLN.

claim: OT-I T cells recovered from draining LN were largely differentiated effectors based on interferon-γ production.
source: These OT-I cells were largely differentiated effectors based on interferon-γ production (Figure 8D).
evidence: Supported by flow cytometric analysis of IFN-γ expression in Figure 8D.

claim: The biased response by L-selectinhi OT-I T cells was not observed outside the primary site of antigen exposure including contralateral LN (cLN) or spleen.
source: This biased response by L-selectinhi OT-I T cells was not observed outside the primary site of antigen exposure including contralateral LN (cLN) or spleen (Figure 8C).
evidence: Supported by in vivo competitive activation assay data in Figure 8C showing no bias in cLN or spleen.

claim: The profound discrepancy between antigen responsiveness of L-selectinhi versus L-selectinint/lo OT-I T cells in vitro and in vivo (2:1 versus 70:1 ratio, respectively) supports a model in which MDSC operate at distal sites to subvert adaptive immunity by restricting L-selectin-directed access of naive CD8+ T cells to cognate antigens within the LN microenvironment.
source: Taken together, the profound discrepancy between antigen responsiveness of L-selectinhi versus L-selectinint/lo OT-I T cells in vitro and in vivo (2:1 versus 70:1 ratio, respectively; Figure 8B and C) supports a model in which MDSC operate at distal sites (i.e., blood and spleen compartments) to subvert adaptive immunity by restricting L-selectin-directed access of naive CD8+ T cells to cognate antigens within the LN microenvironment (Figure 9).
evidence: Inference based on comparison of in vitro and in vivo competitive activation assay results.

claim: Regional LN are major lines of defense against cancer, serving as hubs for the generation of acute antitumor adaptive immunity and durable memory.
source: Regional LN are major lines of defense against cancer, serving as hubs for the generation of acute antitumor adaptive immunity and durable memory.
evidence: Statement of established knowledge about LN function in cancer immunity.

claim: A rate-limiting step for immune surveillance involves trafficking at HEV which ensures that DC present cognate antigens to a sufficiently diverse repertoire of naïve T cells in order to drive expansion of CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cell pools and B cell antibody production.
source: A rate-limiting step for immune surveillance involves trafficking at HEV which ensures that DC present cognate antigens to a sufficiently diverse repertoire of naïve T cells in order to drive expansion of CD4+ and CD8+ effector T cell pools and B cell antibody production (Girard et al., 2012; Evans et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Girard et al., 2012; Evans et al., 2015) documenting importance of HEV trafficking.

claim: Two independent but complementary mechanisms are proposed to reduce LN trafficking in cancer: (1) MDSC-directed downregulation of lymphocyte L-selectin which negatively impacts homing in HEV, and (2) elevated circulating sL-selectin which functions as a competitive antagonist of L-selectin-directed lymphocyte homing in vivo.
source: Accordingly, two independent but complementary mechanisms are proposed to reduce LN trafficking in cancer: (1) MDSC-directed downregulation of lymphocyte L-selectin which we showed negatively impacts homing in HEV, and (2) elevated circulating sL-selectin which, at the concentrations detected in tumor-bearing mice (1 µg/mL in tumor-bearing mice compared to ~0.4 µg/mL in tumor-free controls), reportedly functions as a competitive antagonist of L-selectin-directed lymphocyte homing in vivo.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental findings of L-selectin downregulation and elevated sL-selectin.
